title: Stapleton: heretics’ faith-certainty vs Catholics’ hope-certainty; moral certainty suffices for peace
source_text: XIII. Similia docet Thomas Stapletonus, lib. 9. de Justif. cap. 11. Hoc, inquit, in loco fidei certitudo quam ponunt haeretici, a spei certitudine, quam ponunt Catholici, diligenter distinguenda est; ut ita intelligatur, an negando certitudinem fidei, sinamus fideles in perpetuis dubitationibus; sicuti ergo spes a fide, sic & certitudo spei a certitudine fidei distinguitur. Fides soli verbo Dei nititur tanquam suo proprio objecto, ideoque certitudo fidei ex verbo Dei nascitur, sine ulla consideratione ullius qualitatis ex parte credentis. Verum enim est quod fides dicit, qualiscunque ille sit, vel qualicunque affectu sit qui credit. Itaque haec certitudo est prorsus & omni modo infallibilis. Spes autem nititur non solum verbo Dei, sed etiam studio humano & diligentia per Christi gratiam praestita: ideoque ejus certitudo ex utroque nascitur. Itaque certitudo ejus, ex parte verbi & promissionis Dei, non minor est quam certitudo fidei; ex parte autem conditionis sperantis hominis, dubia & infirma est. Et postquam aliquot argumentis ostendit spem fidelium non niti sola promissione Dei, sed etiam propria fidelis cujusque dispositione, subjungit, Pendet ergo certitudo spei non solum a promissionibus divinis, (ex qua parte est firmissima non secus quam certitudo fidei) sed etiam a conditione & dispositione nostra qui speramus: & ex hac parte licet spei certitudo certitudine fidei minor sit, (quia de nostra dispositione legitima ex fide certi esse non possumus sine speciali revelatione,) tamen non est dubitatio aliqua fluctuans modo in hanc partem, modo in illam, secundum quam modo se acceptum Deo, modo non acceptum aliquis cogitet, alternantibus ex aequo sententiis, semperque anxius & suspensus, id est, neutri parti firmiter assentiens; ut haeretici nos docere mentiuntur: sed est certitudo ex parte subjecti certa & firma, qualis est certitudo omnis moralis, quae magnis argumentis gravique authoritate nititur, quaeque ad animi quietem & tranquillitatem plane sufficit.
pass_a_gloss: Thomas Stapleton teaches similar things in On Justification, book 9, chapter 11. This, he says, in the place of the certainty of faith which the heretics posit, is carefully to be distinguished from the certainty of hope which the Catholics posit; so that it may be understood whether by denying the certainty of faith we leave the faithful in perpetual doubts; just as therefore hope is distinguished from faith, so also the certainty of hope from the certainty of faith. Faith rests on God’s word alone as its proper object, and therefore the certainty of faith is born from God’s word without any consideration of any quality on the believer’s side. For what faith says is true, whatever sort of person he is, or with whatever affection he who believes is. And so this certainty is altogether and in every way infallible. But hope rests not only on God’s word but also on human endeavor and diligence performed through Christ’s grace: and therefore its certainty is born from both. And so its certainty, on the side of the word and promise of God, is not less than the certainty of faith; but on the side of the condition of the hoping person it is doubtful and weak. And after he has shown by several arguments that the hope of the faithful does not rest on God’s promise alone but also on each believer’s own disposition, he adds: Therefore the certainty of hope depends not only on the divine promises (from which side it is most firm no less than the certainty of faith) but also on our condition and disposition who hope: and from this side, although the certainty of hope is less than the certainty of faith (because we cannot be certain from faith of our legitimate disposition without special revelation), yet it is not some fluctuating doubt now to this side, now to that, according to which someone thinks himself now accepted by God, now not accepted, with opinions alternating equally, and always anxious and suspended, that is, firmly assenting to neither side—as the heretics falsely say we teach; but it is a certainty on the subject’s side sure and firm, such as is every moral certainty, which rests on great arguments and weighty authority, and which plainly suffices for quiet and tranquillity of mind.
pass_b_english: Stapleton distinguishes Protestant ‘faith-certainty’ of pardon from Catholic hope-certainty.
Hope is infallible on God’s promise, weaker about one’s disposition, yet still a firm moral certainty—not endless anxious fluctuation.
